resurrect

/rez-uh-REKT/ — stress on REKT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To resurrect something is to bring it back after it seemed to be finished, forgotten, or dead.

Every Thanksgiving, Grandpa resurrects his famous ghost stories from years past.

Example

The film director decided to resurrect the abandoned noir mystery series from the 1950s, filming brand-new episodes with a modern budget and contemporary cinematography.

Resurrect = re (again) + surgere (Latin: to rise; past stem surrect-) = to rise again. The series had effectively died—abandoned and forgotten for decades—and now is being brought back to active existence. Same root as surge and insurgent.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

renew: To renew is to begin something again with fresh energy while it is still alive — you renew a library card, a promise, a friendship that never really ended. To resurrect is stronger: bringing back something that had truly finished or been forgotten. Renewal continues what exists; resurrecting raises what was gone.

reinstate: To reinstate is to put something or someone officially back in place — a suspended player, a canceled rule, a dropped class. It is formal and procedural, reversing a decision. To resurrect is more dramatic: it brings back something that seemed dead and forgotten, not merely paused or set aside on paper.

recreate: To recreate something is to build a fresh copy of it — a museum recreates a colonial kitchen, a movie set recreates 1920s Paris. The original stays gone; only a likeness appears. To resurrect is to bring the original itself back: the actual show, the actual tradition, alive and running again.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bury: put away for good, out of sight

abandon: give up on something permanently

Where it sits · how fully it comes back to life

recall → rekindle → revive → resurrect

recall vs. resurrect: You might recall an old song fondly for a moment, but to resurrect it is to bring it fully back to life on stage.

rekindle vs. resurrect: Rekindling stirs a faded feeling back up — an old passion warming again — but to resurrect something everyone thought was dead and finished takes far more.

revive vs. resurrect: Reviving a tired tradition freshens it up, while resurrecting one means raising it back from the dead entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: again (Latin)

Root — surrect: to rise (past stem of surgere) (Latin)

Put it together: Re- (again) + surrect- (risen, from Latin surgere, to rise) means 'to rise again' — to bring something back up after it seemed dead, finished, or forgotten.

Use the root in a new word: surge: A surge of excitement ran through the crowd the moment the stadium lights came on.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal/literary

Resurrect is the right word when something has truly ended, disappeared, or been forgotten, and you're bringing it back to active existence. For gentler comebacks or routine renewals, revive or renew are often more accurate.
